name: Henna brows

lead: Henna brows use a plant-based paste to stain the brow hairs and the skin underneath, giving darker, more filled-in, defined brows with no tattoo involved. The stain is visible immediately.

Lawsone, the dye in henna, binds to keratin in hair and skin once the dried leaves are powdered and made into a paste. Skin stains typically fade by exfoliation within one to three weeks, and no clinical studies of the brow treatment were found.

paras: It is a short salon service where the paste is applied to the brows and left on before being removed. Results are temporary, so people repeat it every few weeks, often alongside regular brow trimming and shaping.

Pure henna rarely causes reactions, but additives in commercial pastes have been linked to them. Products sold as 'black henna' may contain PPD, which can cause severe allergic reactions and scarring. G6PD deficiency is a noted danger, and the FDA has not approved henna for direct skin use.

chain: Plant dye stains brow hair and skin
angle.text: Henna stains the brow hairs and the skin beneath them, so brows look darker, fuller and more defined straight away. The stain lasts days to weeks and is a surface effect you can see directly.

lead: Henna brows are a salon service in which a paste made from henna, a plant dye, is applied to the eyebrow hairs and the skin beneath them to darken, define and fill the brows. People get them for a fuller, more defined brow that holds colour for weeks, reducing the need for daily brow pencil, and because the stain on the skin makes sparse areas look filled in.[1][2][3]

Henna's staining agent is lawsone, released when the leaves are crushed into a paste; it binds to proteins in the outer skin and hair.[1] Henna has recently been used as a temporary substitute for eyebrow pencil, according to Wikipedia.[1] Unlike regular brow tints, henna contains no peroxide, and the paste is left on for about 10 to 15 minutes, brow artist Amy Jean told Beauty Crew.[2]

The skin stain typically lasts two to three weeks, and hair colour generally lasts three to six weeks depending on the dye and aftercare.[2][3] Some artists combine henna on the skin for a shadow effect with regular tint on the hairs.[2] The main documented hazard is adulterated 'black henna' containing para-phenylenediamine (PPD).[1]

paras: Henna is a dye from the leaves of the henna plant, long used for body decoration and hair colouring. The paste releases dye for only a limited period after preparation, and natural paste is reported to lose staining ability after about a week [1]. Applied to the brows, it stains hair and skin, and practitioners use it to give a fuller, more defined look. Shade depends on the starting hair colour and the product; hair results range from orange to burgundy, and henna is sometimes blended with other plant dyes such as indigo to reach browner or darker tones [1].

Beauty Crew quotes Jazz Pampling noting that henna usually leans warm, with red or orange undertones, and that it will not look natural where there is no hair because the texture is missing.[2] Harper's Bazaar Singapore reports that tinting matches the natural brow colour, will not fill sparse areas, and is painless and cheaper than microblading.[3]

On skin, the stain begins orange and darkens to reddish brown over about three days, then fades as the skin exfoliates, usually within one to three weeks.[1] Amy Jean says brow henna usually lasts two to three weeks and fades faster with oily skin or strong active skincare ingredients.[2] Harper's Bazaar Singapore says tinted colour generally lasts three to six weeks with touch-ups every four to six weeks, and that exfoliating and oil-based products make it fade faster.[3]

Salon artists shape the brow before applying the paste, and Amy Jean advises choosing a qualified artist and checking their before-and-after photos and advises against DIY kits because accuracy matters for shape.[2] Fashion press describes henna as suited to people who want a low-maintenance look without daily brow makeup.[2]

Pure henna is reported to rarely cause problems, with mild reactions usually tied to ingredients such as lemon juice or essential oils [1]. Commercial pastes may contain undisclosed additives linked to allergic reactions [1]. 'Black henna' often contains no henna and may contain PPD in high concentrations; reactions can appear days later, may cause scarring, and PPD sensitisation can be lifelong [1]. The article reports that the US FDA has not approved henna for direct skin application, allowing it only as a hair dye [1]. Henna is also described as dangerous for people with G6PD deficiency [1].

Harper's Bazaar Singapore, citing an expert, names allergic reactions and infections as the main concerns and recommends a patch test; it also says brow dyes are not FDA-approved and advises against using hair dye on brows because its formula can be dangerous near the eyes.[3] Black henna pastes may contain 10 to 80 percent PPD, compared with a hair-dye limit below 6 percent, and reactions can appear 3 to 12 days after application.[1]
